docs.title: Cover Logic
docs.text:
Most blind automations are a pile of "if this, then that" rules, and they work until the day two of them disagree about the same window. Cover Logic replaces that pile with a single decision: you describe your blinds, the modes your house can be in, and the rules for each — and one engine decides where every blind should be, every time, with a record of which rule decided it and why. Because the decision is data rather than scattered automations, you can read it, test it, and move it to a different house. If you have ever lost an afternoon to "why did that blind just close?", this is aimed squarely at you.

It is a Home Assistant custom integration. Nothing is stored outside your Home Assistant instance and nothing leaves it.

docs.title: How a decision gets made
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[House state] --> B[Mode]
    B --> C[Zone rules]
    C --> D[Guards]
    D --> E[Planner]
    E --> F[Cover services]

House state (sensors, helpers, the sun) decides the active mode; the mode and each zone together pick a list of rules, first match wins; the result passes through guards, the interlocks that can drop or delay a blind for reasons that are not really decisions — an open door, a storm, a sauna still running; what survives goes to the planner, which turns one target position and tilt into the ordered cover.* service calls a real motor needs. Every step of that chain is visible afterwards on sensor.cover_logic_mode, including the planner's own output as last_command.

docs.title: What makes it different
docs.text:
Cover Logic adaptive-cover Scope Several zones and modes for a whole house in one config entry One instance per window or cover group Decision First-match rules you write, in plain YAML or the UI A fixed sun-position algorithm per cover type Safety interlocks guards: — skip, defer or force a blind for doors, wind, a running sauna None built in Rollout Shadow mode: decides and logs, moves nothing until you flip dry_run off No dry-run mode documented Why did it do that? sensor.cover_logic_mode's trace names the exact rule No decision trace among its entities Noisy sensors A numeric_state condition can debounce with for: and latch the result for the day Fixed delta-position/delta-time throttling Setting up one window More to configure Simpler — built for exactly this What you can see One diagnostic sensor A target-position sensor, sun start/end times, a "sun in front of window" binary sensor, and more, per instance

adaptive-cover is the better fit for "decide one window's shading automatically" out of the box; Cover Logic is built for "decide every cover in the house from one set of rules, and know why it decided that."

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• New install: install → first setup → shadow mode.
  • Coming from a hand-written automation or another cover integration: the migrate how-to.
  • Understand the model before writing rules: concepts.
  • Something did not move the way you expected: troubleshooting.

docs.title: Why did this blind move, or not move?
docs.text:
Start with sensor.cover_logic_mode's trace attribute — it names the exact rule (mode.zone#index) that decided every blind's current target, including #none for "nothing matched". If the label is not the one you expected to fire, the question becomes "why didn't my rule match", which is usually a condition that is not reading what you think it is reading, or an earlier rule in the same list matching first. If the label is mode.*#index rather than mode.zone#index, the zone fell through to the mode's shared default list — see rules: inherited defaults.

If trace looks right but the blind still did not physically move, work through the cases below in order — they are the three places a decided action can still fail to become a command.

docs.title: The blind never appears in the log at all
docs.text:
If nine blinds get a log line on a recompute and one does not, that missing one is the tell — not an error message, just silence. Check sensor.cover_logic_mode's readiness.blocked attribute for that blind's entity id. If it is there, the list beside it names which entities this blind's own decision depends on that are currently unreadable (absent, unknown, or unavailable, and read by a node with no stated default:). This is a veto, not a timeout — the engine still decided something, and targets/trace still show it, but the executor refuses to act on a decision made from a world it could not fully read. Fix the underlying entity (restore it, wait for it to populate after startup) and the veto lifts on the next evaluation with no further action needed.

A readiness.missing entity with no blind named in readiness.blocked is still worth checking — it means something in the configuration reads an unready entity that happens not to gate any blind yet, which is still usually worth fixing before it does.

docs.title: The blind is waiting and did not move
docs.text:
Check pending.deferred for the blind's entity id. If it is there, a defer-policy guard is holding it: the attribute names which guard, how long it has waited, and what happens when max_wait runs out (proceed or abandon). This is expected, working behaviour for a guard like the one in door interlock — the blind is not stuck, it is correctly waiting for the condition that is deferring it (an open door, a running sauna, whatever the guard watches) to clear.

Also check pending.queued — a blind already mid-sequence (a position move still running, with a tilt move queued behind it) will not react to a new decision until that sequence finishes or is superseded; step shows how far through it is.

docs.title: The blind moved once by hand, and now ignores the configuration
docs.text:
Check manual_holds for the blind's entity id. If it is there, someone (or something with a user_id on its context) moved this blind directly, and manual_detection.hold is deliberately withholding the rule-decided target until the mode or that target changes — usually at the next mode switch, which releases the hold even if the new mode decides the same target. This is the feature working as intended, not a bug: re-sending the old target on every recompute is exactly what hold exists to prevent. Holds are kept in memory only, so a Home Assistant restart or an integration reload also clears them.

If a blind moved by voice is not being held at all even though hold is on, see manual moves: the voice limitation — this is a known Home Assistant limitation this integration cannot see around, not a misconfiguration.

docs.title: I changed the configuration and nothing happened
docs.text:
Editing through the UI or importing a YAML file schedules an automatic reload a couple of seconds after the last write settles — you should not need to reload the integration by hand for an ordinary configuration edit. If a change genuinely does not seem to be taking effect:

  1. Give it a few seconds. A burst of writes (an import touching many subentries, several quick edits in a row) coalesces into one reload after the writes stop, not one reload per write.
  2. Confirm via trace, not by re-reading the configuration. The subentries on screen can be exactly what you intended and the running decision can still be built from an older Config object if the reload has not happened yet — trace is generated by whatever configuration is actually loaded right now, so a label that still reflects the old rule names or the old zone structure is the proof a reload has not landed, independent of what the options screens show you.
  3. Check Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic for a Reload option if you suspect a reload never got scheduled at all — this forces the same reload by hand.
  4. One option is read only at the moment the integration starts up, not live: the Fixture to compare against path (Configure → Execution). Changing it still schedules the same automatic reload as any other configuration write, so the sequence above applies to it too — but if you are specifically troubleshooting fixture drift and just changed that path, give the reload the same few seconds before concluding the comparison is wrong.

dry_run and dead_band, by contrast, are read live from the entry's options on every evaluation and never need a reload at all — if one of those two seems not to have taken effect, the more likely explanation is that the change was not actually saved, not that it needs more time.

docs.title: Blinds
docs.text:
A blind is one physical cover.* entity: the thing the engine decides a position and tilt for. Everything else in the config — zones, rules, guards — refers to blinds by their entity, never by a second id of their own.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.living_room_balcony
    facade_azimuth: 180 # south -- 0 is north, measured clockwise
    tolerance: 40 # sun counts as "on this facade" from 140 to 220 degrees
    travel_time: 45 # seconds for a full run, top to bottom
  - entity: cover.kitchen_window
    has_tilt: false # roller blind, no slat axis at all
zones:
  living_room:
    members: [cover.living_room_balcony]
  kitchen:
    members: [cover.kitchen_window]
modes:
  - id: home
rules: {}

docs.title: Azimuth and the tolerance cone
docs.text:
facade_azimuth is the compass bearing the window's outside faces, in degrees, 0 to 360, measured clockwise from north — the same convention a compass rose is drawn in: 0 is north, 90 is east, 180 is south, 270 is west. tolerance (default 45°) is how far either side of that bearing still counts as "the sun is on this facade", for the sun_hits_target condition. The sector is half-open — [facade_azimuth - tolerance, facade_azimuth + tolerance) — so a sun azimuth of exactly facade_azimuth + tolerance is just outside it.

A blind with no fixed orientation can omit facade_azimuth entirely, at the cost of sun_hits_target never matching it.

A round 90/180/270 is a placeholder, not a measurement

A perfectly round azimuth is a strong signal nobody actually measured the wall — most houses are not built square to the compass. Measure it instead of guessing:

  1. Open a satellite view of the house (any map app with aerial imagery) and draw a line straight out from the window, perpendicular to the wall.
  2. Read the bearing of that line off the map's north arrow, or drop the two endpoints into a bearing calculator.
  3. Cross-check with a compass app held flat against the glass, facing outward — the two should agree within a few degrees.

A wrong azimuth does not fail loudly: sun_hits_target will simply be true or false at the wrong times of day, and nothing else about the configuration looks broken.

docs.title: Travel time and why tilt waits for arrival
docs.text: travel_time (default 60s) is how long a full run takes, used to wait for the position move to finish before sending a tilt command. This matters because a tilt sent during a position move is typically discarded by the motor — the blind arrives at the right height with slats in whatever state they happened to be in. tilt_after_arrival (default true) is what turns this waiting on; set it to false only if your motor genuinely accepts both commands at once. Get travel_time roughly right — a blind that physically takes 55s to close should not be configured with 20s, or the tilt command fires while it is still moving.

docs.title: has_tilt
docs.text: has_tilt (default true) marks whether the cover has a slat/tilt channel at all. A blind with has_tilt: false — a roller blind — should only ever be given a position in its rules; the engine still accepts tilt values for it, but nothing is ever sent for that axis.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Leaving facade_azimuth at a round placeholder instead of measuring it.
  • Setting travel_time far below the blind's real full-travel time, so tilt commands race the position move.
  • Forgetting has_tilt: false on a roller blind, which does not break anything by itself but makes a tilt value in a rule misleading to read.

docs.title: Where to edit this
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Add blind (or Edit blind, from the options menu). The form matches this schema field for field, including slat_distance/slat_depth for a computed slat angle.

See the reference: blinds for every field and its default.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
A guard is a safety interlock: a condition, a policy, and what it covers — evaluated on top of whatever the rules decided. guards is an ordered list; like modes and rules, they resolve first match wins, in written order. There are no numeric priorities.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.living_room_balcony
zones:
  living_room:
    members: [cover.living_room_balcony]
modes:
  - id: home
conditions:
  balcony_door_open:
    condition: state
    entity_id: binary_sensor.balcony_door
    state: "on"
rules:
  home.living_room:
    - then: {position: 0, tilt: 0}
guards:
  - name: do not lower the balcony blind while the door is open
    policy: defer
    applies_to: closing # raising it is always safe; only closing is the hazard
    targets: [living_room]
    when: !ref balcony_door_open
    max_wait: 10800
    on_timeout: abandon
    recheck_every: 900

While the door is open, a close the rule decided is held back; once the door shuts the guard stops matching and the rule's close is sent on that same recompute. One defer guard is the whole interlock — see door interlock for the recipe.

First match wins per blind: for each blind, the first guard (in written order) whose targets cover it, whose applies_to matches and whose when is true decides that blind, and no later guard is asked. Two guards with the same when and overlapping targets therefore never both fire — the second is dead for those blinds.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
• skip — do not move it. The matched axis' whole action is suppressed, tilt included, not just the half the condition is about.
  • defer — move it later. Requires max_wait (null means wait indefinitely — a stated value, not an omission) and on_timeout (proceed: do it anyway once the wait runs out, or abandon: drop it — no default, since the two are opposites and both are in real use).
  • force — move it now, regardless of what the rules decided. Requires then:, the action to impose.
flowchart TD
    G1[Guard #0] -->|matches| Done1[Outcome decided]
    G1 -->|no match| G2[Guard #1]
    G2 -->|matches| Done2[Outcome decided]
    G2 -->|no match| G3[Guard #2 ...]
    G3 -->|no match| None[No guard: the rule's own decision stands]

docs.title: Stage: before or after the decision
docs.text: stage: output (the default) judges the action the rules already decided — it can still see what the engine chose. stage: input drops the target before the engine is even asked, so no decision is made for it at all. An input-stage guard may not set applies_to to anything but any: at that point there is no candidate command yet for "closing" or "opening" to mean anything about.

docs.title: applies_to
docs.text: closing means a decreasing position, and only that — a blind's slats moving are never by themselves the hazard a guard like this exists for. opening is the increasing case; any (the default) does not care which way.

docs.title: A numeric threshold needs a named condition
docs.text: When editing from the UI, a guard's own inline condition selector cannot carry the default a numeric_state needs — Home Assistant's selector rejects that key — so a guard gated on a numeric threshold must reference a named condition instead.

docs.title: max_wait, on_timeout, recheck_every
docs.text:
These three only apply to defer. max_wait is how long the wait may last (seconds, or null for no deadline); on_timeout is what happens when it runs out — proceed sends the held action, abandon logs a warning and sends nothing. Either way the guard keeps holding the blind for as long as its condition stays true, and releases it the moment the condition clears.

A wait survives a Home Assistant restart without a hand-written watchdog because it is not an in-flight timer: it is re-derived from the configuration and the live condition on every evaluation, so the first evaluation after startup recreates it (with waited back at zero, which only ever makes a timeout later). recheck_every (seconds, default 900) is how often an unresolved wait is re-examined even when nothing else changes, and the re-examination is never scheduled past the max_wait deadline, so the timeout applies on time.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing a defer without deciding on_timeout up front — there is no default, and the two choices behave oppositely.
  • Putting a narrower guard after a broader one that already matches everything it would have covered — first match wins, so the narrower one never gets a turn. A skip and a defer with the same when on the same blind are the common case: only the first one written ever fires.
  • Giving an input-stage guard a direction other than any — this is a configuration error, not a silent no-op.

docs.title: Where to edit this
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Add guard. The first screen asks for policy before anything else, because the policy decides which fields the next screen even shows.

See the reference: guards for the full field list.

docs.title: Manual moves
docs.text:
Manual-move detection is how the integration tells "a person just moved this blind by hand" apart from its own commands and from everything else that also changes a cover's state. It is the one part of the configuration the decision engine itself never reads — it only affects what the coordinator does after a decision is already made.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.living_room_balcony
zones:
  living_room:
    members: [cover.living_room_balcony]
modes:
  - id: home
rules: {}
manual_detection:
  ignore_while_on: [script.evening_routine, input_boolean.bulk_move_in_progress]
  hold: true

docs.title: ignore_while_on
docs.text: A list of entities that are only on for the duration of an automated mover's own run — most usefully a script.* entity, which Home Assistant keeps on for exactly as long as that script executes. While any of them is on, a state change on a watched blind is attributed to that run, not to a person — a script inherits the caller's context (including user_id), so without this exclusion a script a person started would look exactly like that person moving the blind directly. It is not restricted to the script. domain: an input_boolean a house sets around its own bulk movements works identically.

docs.title: hold
docs.text:
When true, a blind a person just moved by hand is left alone — the integration stops re-sending that blind's current target on every later recompute. The hold remembers the mode and the target in force when the move was seen, and is released as soon as either changes: a mode switch releases it even when the new mode decides the same target. Guards still act normally on a held blind; only the plain rule-decided outcome is withheld. Without hold, a level-held target (for example "night mode always wants position 0") would be silently re-asserted on the next recompute, undoing a move someone just made from the app seconds earlier.

Holds live in memory only: a Home Assistant restart or a reload of the integration forgets them, and the next recompute sends the decided target again.

docs.title: Why detection needs user_id
docs.text:
A move is only recognised as manual when its state change carries a context.user_id at all. That is a deliberate, narrower test than "this wasn't one of our own commands" — a change with no user_id attached (many automations' and scripts' own commands) is silently discarded rather than assumed to be a person, because the absence of "us" is not evidence of a person either. Three conditions must all hold for a movement to count as manual:

  1. a user_id is present on the new state's context,
  2. it is not one of this integration's own commands (tracked by context, not by user_id alone), and
  3. no entity in ignore_while_on is currently on.

A physical wall switch or a remote wired straight to the motor carries no user_id, so such a move is not detected and hold does not protect it: the next recompute that re-sends the target undoes it. Only moves made from the Home Assistant app or UI (by a logged-in user) are recognised.

docs.title: The voice limitation
docs.text: Home Assistant does not guarantee a user_id on the context of every state change a voice command produces — a command spoken through an Assist satellite can arrive with a context that carries no user_id, depending on the pipeline and integration involved. Because manual-move detection requires user_id to be present at all, a blind moved by voice may not be recognised as a manual move, and hold will not protect it. There is no workaround at the configuration level; this is a property of what Home Assistant attaches to a voice-originated service call, not something manual_detection can see around.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting hold to apply to a guard-driven outcome — it only withholds the plain rule decision; a guard that fires still wins.
  • Forgetting to add a new script that moves blinds in bulk to ignore_while_on — every run will otherwise look like somebody grabbed every blind in the house by hand at once.
  • Assuming a voice-controlled or wall-switch move is covered the same way an app move is — only moves carrying a user_id are detected (see above).

docs.title: Where to edit this
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Manual detection (there is only one instance for the whole house; the menu offers Edit manual detection once it exists).

See the reference: manual_detection for the full field list.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
A mode is the house's overall state — away, night, home, and so on. Exactly one mode is active at a time, and which rules apply depends on the active mode as well as the zone (see rules).

config
blinds: []
zones: {}
conditions:
  house_armed_away:
    condition: state
    entity_id: alarm_control_panel.home_alarm
    state: armed_away
  house_dark:
    condition: sun
    after: sunset
    before: sunrise # before+after sunrise/sunset is the dark window around midnight
modes:
  - id: away
    when: !ref house_armed_away
  - id: night
    when: !ref house_dark
  - id: home # fallback: no `when` at all, and it must be last
rules: {}

docs.title: First match wins
docs.text:
modes is an ordered list. Each mode's when is evaluated top to bottom, and the first one whose condition matches is the active mode — later modes are never even checked, so order encodes priority. away is listed first above because being armed away should outrank being in the dark window, not the other way round.

flowchart TD
    A[Evaluate away.when] -->|true| M1[mode = away]
    A -->|false| B[Evaluate night.when]
    B -->|true| M2[mode = night]
    B -->|false| C[home: no condition]
    C --> M3[mode = home]

docs.title: The last mode has no condition
docs.text:
The last entry in modes must omit when entirely — it is the fallback, guaranteed to match whatever the earlier modes did not. validate() flags this as an error two ways: no_fallback_mode if nothing in the list is condition-less, and fallback_mode_not_last if one exists but something follows it (which could then never run). Choosing no mode at all is not a valid outcome for a configuration — leaving a true fallback off the end is the one requirement every list of modes must satisfy.

A when condition can be any of the dialect's bodies — state, numeric_state, time, sun, template, and/or/not, or a reusable !ref. The diagram below is what a sun-based condition like house_dark actually divides a day into: everything before dawn and after dusk falls into one segment, the rest into another.

A top-level numeric_state also takes a default, used when the compared entity is unavailable or not a number — pick one that fails on the safe side, since the condition is evaluated exactly as if that were the entity's real reading.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Putting the fallback mode anywhere but last.
  • Giving two modes overlapping conditions and relying on list order to break the tie without checking which one is actually listed first.
  • Forgetting that a mode id may not contain a . — it is joined with the zone id as f"{mode}.{zone}" to look up rules, and a dot would make that join ambiguous.

docs.title: Where to edit this
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Add mode (or Edit mode). The options menu also has a read-only report of modes and rules in their real evaluation order, useful for checking first-match-wins ordering without reading YAML.

See the reference: modes for the field list.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
A rule says what a zone's blinds should do, in one mode. rules is a mapping keyed "<mode id>.<zone id>", each value a list of rules evaluated first-match-wins — the same resolution order as modes themselves.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.a
    facade_azimuth: 270
zones:
  terrace:
    members: [cover.a]
modes:
  - {id: night, when: {condition: state, entity_id: input_boolean.cover_down, state: "on"}}
  - {id: home}
values:
  flower_target:
    entity: input_number.flower_position
    default: 34
rules:
  night.terrace:
    - then: {position: 0, tilt: 0}
  home.terrace:
    - if: {condition: numeric_state, entity_id: sensor.wind, default: 0, above: 60}
      then: {position: 100, tilt: 100}
      name: high wind, open fully
    - then: {position: !ref flower_target, tilt: keep}

docs.title: First match, in order
docs.text:
For the resolved mode and each zone, the key f"{mode}.{zone_id}" is looked up and its rule list is tried top to bottom; the first rule whose if matches decides that zone's blinds. A rule with no if matches unconditionally, so it should always be last in its list — anything after it can never fire. No matching rule at all (or no rules: entry for that key) both resolve to "keep both axes", shown in the trace as #none — the two causes look the same on purpose, since debugging either means checking the same things.

flowchart LR
    Mode[Active mode] --> Zone[Zone's own rules, in order]
    Zone -->|first match| Decided[Decided action]
    Zone -->|no match| Default[Mode's default rules: mode.*]
    Default --> Decided
    Decided --> Guards[Guards: may skip, defer or force]
    Guards --> Command[cover.* service call]

docs.title: then: keep or a number, per axis
docs.text:
then is {position?, tilt?}. Each axis is independently:

  • an integer 0–100,
  • keep, meaning leave that axis exactly where it is, or
  • !ref <value name>, read at decision time (see values).

Leaving an axis out of then entirely means the same as keep — a rule then: {position: 100} for a blind with no tilt axis is written exactly like that, nothing else needed.

docs.title: Inherited defaults
docs.text:
A rule list filed under the special zone id * — "<mode id>.*" — applies to every zone in that mode that does not shadow it. A zone's own list is tried in full first; only once nothing in it matches does evaluation fall through to the mode's defaults, also tried in full. This lets a house say "everyone closes at night" once instead of repeating the same rule per zone, while still letting one zone override it with its own list.

# fragment -- "*" is every zone in mode "night" that has no own rules for it
rules:
  "night.*":
    - then: {position: 0, tilt: 0}

docs.title: events
docs.text: events restricts a rule to specific triggering events: state_change (an ordinary recompute), manual_move (a person moved a blind, see manual moves) or arrival. If the event that triggered this evaluation is not in the list, the rule is skipped regardless of its if. The running integration currently produces only state_change and manual_move; arrival is accepted but nothing raises it yet.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Placing a condition-less rule before one that should take priority — it will always win, and the rules after it never run.
  • Forgetting that "*" default rules only apply when a zone's own list has no match at all, not as a merge with it.
  • Using events: to try to limit how often a rule can fire over time — it only filters by which kind of event triggered this evaluation, not by timing.

docs.title: Where to edit this
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Add rule (or Edit rule), after choosing the mode and zone it belongs to. Its order field stands in for YAML list position — lower runs first, suggested ten past the last rule in that list so there is room to insert one later; no two rules in the same mode-and-zone list may share an order. The options menu's "rules in real evaluation order" report shows the full first-match-wins sequence, own rules before defaults, without reading YAML.

See the reference: rules and reference: rule then for the full field list.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
A value is something a rule's position/tilt can read instead of a literal number, referenced with !ref <name>. values is a mapping of name -> body; type (default entity) picks which of the two shapes it is.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.a
    facade_azimuth: 270
    slat_distance: 25 # mm, gap between adjacent slats
    slat_depth: 35 # mm, width of one slat, front to back
zones:
  terrace:
    members: [cover.a]
modes:
  - id: home
values:
  flower_target: # type: entity (the default) -- read a helper at decision time
    entity: input_number.flower_position
    default: 34
  slat_angle: # type: slat_angle -- computed from solar geometry
    type: slat_angle
    default: 50 # used whenever the geometry has no answer
    scale: half
rules:
  home.terrace:
    - then: {position: !ref flower_target, tilt: !ref slat_angle}

docs.title: type: entity
docs.text: Reads a Home Assistant helper at decision time, truncated to an integer — not clamped to 0–100, unlike a literal in a rule. default is required and is what a rule gets back when the entity is missing or unparsable; it is itself range-checked at parse time.

docs.title: type: slat_angle
docs.text:
Computes the tilt percentage that just blocks the direct sun beam, using the blind being decided's own facade_azimuth, slat_distance and slat_depth — one slat_angle value serves every facade in the house, each blind supplying its own geometry. scale: half (the default) maps 0–90° of slat rotation to 0–100%; scale: full maps the full 0–180°.

default here is returned whenever the geometry has no answer at all — the sun is down, off this facade, the blind states no slat_distance/ slat_depth, or the slats cannot block the beam at that elevation — never an error, always the stated fallback. Unlike an entity value, the computed result is clamped to 0–100 before it reaches the rule, because degrees past the slat's own travel are not a position the hardware has.

The slat direction is unverified

The formula gives a high percentage for a high sun. Whether tilt: 100 means "slats flat/open" or "slats steep/closed" depends on your motor's own convention, and that mapping has not been confirmed against real hardware in practice. Before relying on slat_angle for anything, test it on one blind: set a rule to tilt: !ref slat_angle, watch what the slats actually do as the sun moves, and only then roll it out to the rest of the house. Measure slat_distance/slat_depth on the blind itself, once per slat type — not guessed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using type: entity without a sane default — a helper that resets to 0 after a restart (no initial:) will silently drive every rule that reads it until someone notices.
  • Expecting slat_angle to also decide height — it never does; see rules for position, which slat_angle leaves alone.
  • Rolling slat_angle out to every facade before confirming the tilt direction on one blind (see the warning above).

docs.title: Where to edit this
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Add value (or Edit value). scale only appears once type: slat_angle is selected — the form adapts to the chosen type.

See the reference: values (entity) and reference: values (type: slat_angle) for the full field list.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
A zone is a group of blinds decided together. Rules are never written against an individual blind — they are written against a zone, one rule list per (mode, zone) pair, and every blind in that zone gets the same answer for a given rule.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.bedroom_window
  - entity: cover.office_window
zones:
  bedroom:
    members: [cover.bedroom_window]
    occupants: [alex]
  office:
    members: [cover.office_window]
modes:
  - id: home
rules: {}

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
• members — the blind entity ids decided together as this zone.
  • occupants — person names (as in person.<name>) read by the event_targets_zone condition. A zone with no occupants simply never matches that condition (and the running integration raises no person events yet, so for now no zone does).

docs.title: One zone per blind
docs.text:
Every blind must belong to exactly one zone:

  • A blind claimed by two zones has no answer — whose rules should apply is unanswerable — so the config fails to evaluate at all (EngineError, reported as a validation error before that).
  • A blind claimed by no zone is skipped, not fatal: everything else still gets decided, and a blind_without_zone validation warning calls it out so it does not go unnoticed. Nothing will ever move that blind until it is added to a zone.

That asymmetry is deliberate: "two owners" has no correct guess to fall back on, while "no owner" does — leave it alone and say so loudly.

# fragment -- this blind is defined but assigned to no zone.
# validate() reports "blind_without_zone"; nothing ever moves it.
blinds:
  - entity: cover.garage_door
zones:
  office:
    members: [cover.office_window] # garage_door is not a member anywhere

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Adding a blind's entity to blinds: and forgetting to add it to a zone's members: — it parses fine and is silently never decided.
  • Listing the same blind under two zones' members: — this is a hard error, not a warning, because there is no rule that says which zone wins.
  • Expecting occupants: to filter which rules in the zone can fire — it only feeds event_targets_zone; every other condition in the zone's rules evaluates normally regardless of who lives there.

docs.title: Where to edit this
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Add zone (or Edit zone). The picker for members only offers blinds already added under Add blind.

See the reference: zones for the full field list.

docs.title: First setup
docs.text:
Once the integration is added, it shows one menu: How do you want to start?

Choice What it does Set up blinds now (recommended) Pick your cover entities, say which way each one faces, and it builds a working configuration for you. Load a configuration from a YAML file Point it at a file on disk — the same format import_config reads. For moving a configuration from another house, or restoring one written by hand. Start from the example configuration Imports docs/example-config.yaml, a complete worked example for an invented two-bedroom apartment — a plausible starting point to read and edit rather than an empty one. Only offered when that file ships alongside the install. Start empty A config entry with no subentries at all. You build everything by clicking afterwards.

Every choice ends with a usable entry. "Start empty" is a deliberate exception to "usable": it has no fallback mode yet, so the entry sits in a not ready state (visible on the integration's card) until you add a mode with no condition — normal for a fresh, empty entry, not an error to chase.

docs.title: Walkthrough: "Set up blinds now"
docs.text: This is the three-screen flow behind the recommended choice.

docs.title: 1. Pick your covers
docs.text: Blinds — an entity picker, filtered to the cover domain. Pick every cover.* you want Cover Logic to decide for. You can add more blinds later from the options menu; nothing here is final.

docs.title: 2. Say which way each one faces
docs.text: One screen per blind picked, asked in turn: "{blind} — pick the compass direction its outside faces." This decides when the sun reaches it — see blinds for what facade_azimuth actually does with the answer. Guessing is fine for now; the SVG and the measurement method on that page explain how to get a real reading later.

docs.title: 3. Review the summary, then create it
docs.text:
Before anything is saved, the flow lists the blinds you picked and summarises what it is about to build:

At night nothing moves; by day each blind shades (position 20, tilt 45) when the sun is on its side, else stays open (100).

Concretely, this is one zone holding every blind you picked, two modes (day when sun.sun is above_horizon, night as the fallback), and two rules per mode shared by that zone: shade on sun_hits_target, otherwise stay open; at night, keep/keep for everything. It is a real, working configuration from the first screen — not a placeholder you must finish before anything happens — and every part of it (the zone, the modes, the rules, the blinds' own facing) can be edited afterwards from Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Configure.

Confirming creates the entry. Cancelling returns to the main menu with nothing saved.

docs.title: What to do next
docs.text: The entry is created with dry_run on, so nothing will actually move yet — see shadow mode for what that means and the checklist for turning it off. To reshape what "Set up blinds now" built — splitting one zone into several, adding a guard, naming a reusable value — see the concepts pages and the how-to guides.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: Cover Logic is not in the HACS default store yet, so add it as a custom repository, or copy the files in by hand. Either way, it ends up as one custom integration under custom_components/cover_logic/.

docs.title: Via HACS
docs.text:
1. HACS → ⋮ (top right) → Custom repositories.
  2. URL: https://github.com/PeterLinuxOSS/ha-cover-logic, category Integration.
  3. Find "Cover Logic" in HACS and download it.
  4. Restart Home Assistant.
  5. Settings → Devices & services → Add Integration → "Cover Logic".

docs.title: Without HACS
docs.text:
1. Copy custom_components/cover_logic/ from this repository into your Home Assistant's own custom_components/ directory, so the result is <config>/custom_components/cover_logic/.
  2. Restart Home Assistant.
  3. Settings → Devices & services → Add Integration → "Cover Logic".

docs.title: Single instance
docs.text: Cover Logic supports exactly one config entry per Home Assistant instance — adding it a second time is refused before the setup menu even appears. A multi-house or multi-floor setup is expressed with zones and modes inside that one entry, not with a second entry.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Setup asks how you want to start — see first setup for the four choices and a walkthrough of the recommended one.

docs.title: Shadow mode
docs.text:
Cover Logic decides from the moment it is set up, whether or not it is allowed to act on that decision. dry_run is what separates the two, and it is on by default. While it is on, every command is decided, planned, queued and logged — and nothing is sent to a real cover.* service. A fresh install therefore moves nothing, even though sensor.cover_logic_mode is already reporting a mode and a target for every blind.

This is the intended way to start: install it alongside whatever already controls your blinds (existing automations, adaptive-cover, a hand-written script), watch what Cover Logic would have done, compare it against what actually happened, and only then hand it the covers for real.

docs.title: Where to toggle it
docs.text:
Settings → Devices & services → Cover Logic → Configure → Execution. This one screen holds the integration's three options — settings stored on the entry itself rather than as configuration subentries:

  • Dry run — on: nothing moves, every intended command is written to the log. Off: covers really move. Takes effect immediately, with no reload, so "turn the hands off right now" never has to wait for one.
  • Fixture to compare against — an optional path to a YAML file the drift check compares the live configuration against. Empty means a fixtures/ directory beside custom_components/, or no comparison at all if there is none. Most installs leave it empty. Changing it reloads the integration by itself.
  • Dead band — how many points a cover's reported position or tilt may differ from a rule's target before Cover Logic bothers to send a command. Also used as the tolerance for deciding a move has arrived. Default 5. Too small, and a blind whose motor slightly mis-reports its own position after moving gets re-sent the same command for no reason — tilting a blind's slats shifts the motor's own position estimate, so a repeated absolute command is itself an unwanted movement. Too large, and the integration stops correcting real drift. If one blind's tilt motor under-reports further than the rest of the house after a move (watch last_command for a suppressed entry that looks wrong), raise this rather than chasing the individual blind.

Dry run and dead band are read live from the running entry — no reload needed for either.

docs.title: What the log looks like while dry
docs.text: Every command — dry or real — is written in the same shape, so comparing against /api/logbook or whatever automation you are replacing is the whole point of the exercise. The newest one is also always available as last_command on the diagnostic sensor, without tailing anything.

docs.title: Checklist before turning it off
docs.text:
Work through all four before flipping Dry run off. None of them need the log tailed in real time — read them back from sensor.cover_logic_mode's attributes and the logbook after the fact.

  1. trace names your own zones, not a default. Every entry should read like night.terrace#0, not night.*#0 — a * means that pair fell through to a mode's shared default list rather than the zone-specific rules you expect. Seeing * where you expected a named zone usually means the rule you wrote was never saved, or was saved for a different zone id than the blind's own.
  2. matica_diff is [], if you are migrating off something this sensor can be compared against (the old system this project itself replaced exposed one). An empty list means "checked, and they agree"; null means there is nothing to compare against at all — read sensor reference for the difference between those two.
  3. No open repair issues under Settings → System → Repairs — see repairs for what each one means and how to clear it. None of the four are fatal to dry-run operation, but every one means some blind is not being decided the way you think it is.
  4. Watch one dusk and one morning in the log. These are the two moments most configurations have the most rules firing in the shortest time — mode switches, guards releasing, dead-band skips all happening together. A quiet daytime log proves far less than fifteen minutes of a real sunset.

Once all four are satisfied, flip Dry run off from the same Execution screen. Nothing else changes — the same rules, the same guards, the same trace — only the services actually go out.

docs.title: Never close a blind onto an open door
docs.text:
A blind mounted over a door — a terrace, a balcony — must never be driven down while that door is open, and should close itself once the door shuts again. One defer guard does both; this page is the practical recipe for that common case, and guards covers the mechanism in depth.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.terrace_door
    facade_azimuth: 180
zones:
  terrace:
    members: [cover.terrace_door]
conditions:
  terrace_door_open:
    condition: state
    entity_id: binary_sensor.terrace_door
    state: "on"
modes:
  - id: home
rules:
  home.terrace:
    - then: {position: 0, tilt: 0} # this zone's normal rule: closed
guards:
  - name: do not lower the terrace blind while the door is open
    policy: defer
    applies_to: closing
    targets: [terrace]
    when: !ref terrace_door_open
    max_wait: 10800
    on_timeout: abandon
    recheck_every: 900

docs.title: How the one guard does both jobs
docs.text:
While the door is open and the rule wants the blind lower than it is now, the guard fires and the blind is held: no command is sent. Holding is the "never onto an open door" half.

The guard is re-evaluated on every recompute, and the door sensor is one of the entities the integration watches, so the door shutting triggers a recompute by itself. At that moment the guard's condition is false, the wait is released, and the rule's own decision — closed — is sent like any other. That is the "close it once the door shuts" half. Nothing has to remember the close: it is simply what the rule still decides.

applies_to: closing keeps the guard out of everything else. Raising the blind, or moving only its slats, is never held, and a blind that is already closed is not "closing", so opening the door under it holds nothing.

Do not add a skip guard with the same when in front of this one. Guards are first match wins per blind, so the skip would take every case and the defer would never fire — and with it, pending.deferred would stay empty and max_wait would never be counted.

docs.title: Choosing max_wait and on_timeout
docs.text:
max_wait: 10800 (three hours, what the author's own house uses) is how long the guard waits before its timeout answer applies. The two answers are opposites and there is no default:

  • abandon — the wait gives up: a warning is logged and nothing is sent. The guard still fires while the door stays open, so the blind keeps waiting, and it still closes when the door finally shuts. In practice abandon stops the periodic re-examination and leaves a log line saying the door was open unusually long.
  • proceed — the held close is sent once the deadline passes, onto the open door. This is rarely what you want for a door.

max_wait: null waits with no deadline at all: no timeout ever applies, and the blind closes when the door shuts, however long that takes.

docs.title: Watching it work
docs.text: While the door is open and a close is being held, the diagnostic sensor's pending.deferred attribute has an entry for cover.terrace_door: the guard's index and name, state (waiting, then abandon or proceed once max_wait has run out), waited and max_wait in seconds, on_timeout and recheck_every. The entry disappears when the door shuts. A blind over an open door with no entry is one the rule does not currently want lower — nothing is being held. See troubleshooting for the full walkthrough.

docs.title: Restart safety
docs.text: Nothing above needs a watchdog script. A deferral is re-derived from the configuration and the live door state on every evaluation rather than kept as an in-flight timer, so a Home Assistant restart cannot cancel it: the first evaluation after startup recreates the wait if the door is still open, or sends the close if it shut in the meantime. recheck_every (900 s here, also the default) makes an unresolved wait re-examine itself even when nothing changes, so the timeout is applied on time — the re-examination is scheduled no later than the max_wait deadline. The only cost of a restart is that waited starts again from zero, which only ever moves the timeout later, never earlier.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Pairing this defer with a skip guard on the same door — see above; the first one written takes every case.
  • Setting applies_to: any instead of closing — this would also hold the blind from opening while the door is open, which is never the hazard a door interlock exists for.
  • Forgetting on_timeout — there is no default, and a config that omits it is rejected rather than silently picking one.

docs.title: Decide dusk from a lux sensor
docs.text:
A lux sensor looks like the obvious way to decide "is it dark enough to close for the night" — more direct than a fixed clock time, and it adapts to an overcast day on its own. It is also the condition type most likely to misbehave if written as a plain threshold, for two independent reasons this page covers in order: noise at the threshold, and a sensor that does not move much at all.

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.terrace_door
zones:
  terrace:
    members: [cover.terrace_door]
conditions:
  dusk:
    condition: numeric_state
    entity_id: sensor.outdoor_illuminance
    below: 2800
    for: 180
    latch: daily
    default: 99999
modes:
  - id: night
    when: !ref dusk
  - id: home
rules:
  night.terrace:
    - then: {position: 0, tilt: 0}
  home.terrace:
    - then: {position: keep, tilt: keep}

docs.title: Why default: 99999, not a low number
docs.text: numeric_state requires an explicit default (see the conditions reference). For a "below" threshold, the default has to be a value that fails the comparison, so a missing or unavailable sensor reads as broad daylight rather than as dusk — the opposite mistake to heatwave's default, but the same principle: pick the default that means "nothing unusual", never the one that happens to be convenient to type.

docs.title: Why a plain threshold is not enough: for:
docs.text:
A numeric_state condition with no for: reacts to every single reading, and most lux sensors rewrite their value every couple of minutes even while sitting still. At dusk the value spends a long stretch hovering right around any fixed threshold, and a sensor that briefly dips below 2800 lux and climbs back up a reading later would otherwise flip the mode twice in the space of four minutes — each flip sending every blind in the zone on a full run. This was measured, not theoretical: on one installation, a lux reading of 2788, then 2813, then 2742 four minutes apart made a terrace door blind close, reopen, and close again in one evening.

for: 180 fixes the obvious half of this: the threshold must stay crossed for three minutes before the condition answers true at all. Note that this for: is not measured the way condition: state's for: is — a numeric_state has no single "last changed" moment to measure from, since the sensor keeps rewriting its value whether or not it has crossed anything. This dialect resolves it from a separate per-threshold memory instead (see "Why hysteresis fails" below for what that memory is for).

docs.title: Why for: alone is still not enough: latch: daily
docs.text:
for: only qualifies the entry — it says a reading has to stay below the threshold for a while before dusk is believed at all. It says nothing about the exit: once genuinely past dusk, the value still sits near the threshold for a long time as the sky keeps darkening, and a single upward wobble an hour after real dusk would otherwise undo it and reopen a house that was correctly closed for the night. Dusk does not un-happen once it has happened.

latch: daily is the other half: once the threshold has genuinely been crossed (survived its for:) today, the condition keeps answering true for the rest of the local day, regardless of what the sensor does afterwards. The reset is the calendar rolling over to a new date, not a second timer to tune.

Neither half works alone. latch: daily with no for: would let a single stray midday reading latch the rest of the day as "dusk" the moment anything dipped the sensor even briefly — latch: only makes sense tied to an entry that has already been debounced. This is checked, not just advised: a configuration with latch: on a condition that is not numeric_state, or with any value other than daily, is a validation error, not a quietly ignored field.

docs.title: Why not hysteresis?
docs.text: The textbook fix for a noisy threshold is hysteresis — a different "off" level than "on" level, so a value has to travel further before flipping back. It does not work here: measured over ten days, this class of lux sensor saturates around 3050 during the day and never once exceeded 3200 in those ten days of measurements, so a hysteresis band wide enough to actually absorb daytime noise would never release again once triggered — the house would stay in "dusk" from roughly midday onward, every day. for: plus latch: daily solves the actual problem (a debounced entry, a remembered exit) without needing the sensor's full dynamic range to have headroom it does not have. Measure your own sensor's daytime ceiling before trying hysteresis on it — a sensor that saturates much lower than its nominal maximum is the warning sign.

docs.title: The latch does not survive a restart
docs.text: The memory for:/latch: need is held in the running coordinator, not written to storage — a Home Assistant restart loses it. In practice this is safe in the direction that matters: after a restart during the latched window, the condition falls back to the plain threshold until it re-earns the latch on its own, which can only ever make the house open later in that edge case, never close early onto a boundary it had not actually crossed. If a restart happens to land in the narrow window between a genuine dusk and the sensor settling comfortably below the threshold, a single wobble could reopen things until the dwell re-qualifies — rare, and strictly a smaller risk than running with no latch at all.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting default to a value that happens to be below the threshold — this makes a dead sensor report dusk immediately, the opposite of a safe failure.
  • Using latch: "Daily", latch: true, or any other spelling — the one accepted value is the literal string daily.
  • Expecting for: here to behave like condition: state's for: — it is resolved from a dedicated dwell, not from World.since, precisely because this entity's value changes constantly.

docs.title: Close blinds during a heatwave
docs.text:
A heatwave rule is a numeric_state condition on an outdoor temperature sensor, used either inside a mode's when (the whole house reacts) or inside a single rule's if (one zone reacts, which is usually what you want — a heatwave is not reason enough to black out a room nobody uses in the daytime).

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.living_room_window
    facade_azimuth: 180
    tolerance: 40
zones:
  living_room:
    members: [cover.living_room_window]
conditions:
  heatwave:
    condition: numeric_state
    entity_id: sensor.outdoor_temperature
    default: 20
    above: 28
  sun_on_this_facade:
    condition: sun_hits_target
values:
  heatwave_tilt:
    entity: input_number.heatwave_tilt_target
    default: 40
modes:
  - id: home
rules:
  home.living_room:
    - if: {condition: and, conditions: [!ref heatwave, !ref sun_on_this_facade]}
      then: {position: keep, tilt: !ref heatwave_tilt}
      name: heatwave shading on the sunlit side, leave height alone
    - then: {position: keep, tilt: keep}

docs.title: default is the most important field here
docs.text: numeric_state requires an explicit default (see the conditions reference). For a heatwave threshold, the default must read as not a heatwave — 20°C above, as here — so a dead or unavailable outdoor temperature sensor never fakes one and closes the whole house. Picking a default that would read as true is a mistake that only shows up the day the sensor actually fails.

docs.title: Only shade the sunlit side
docs.text: Pairing heatwave with sun_hits_target (as above) means the rule only fires for a blind whose own facade the sun is currently on — a heatwave condition alone, with no sun check, shades every blind in the zone regardless of which way it faces, including ones already in shadow that gain nothing from closing. Drop the and/sun_on_this_facade half if you genuinely want every blind in the zone to react the same way regardless of orientation (for example, a single-aspect room).

docs.title: Reading the tilt amount from a helper
docs.text: heatwave_tilt above is a type: entity value, so the shading amount is an input_number you can tune from the dashboard without editing the rule. Use a literal number instead (tilt: 40) if you never expect to change it.

docs.title: Letting it recover automatically
docs.text: Nothing extra is needed for the blind to reopen once the heatwave passes — heatwave simply stops matching once the sensor reads below 28°C, and the catch-all rule (then: {position: keep, tilt: keep}) takes over. If you want it to actively reopen rather than just stop re-closing, give the catch-all a real action (for example tilt: 100) instead of keep.

docs.title: Combining with wind safety
docs.text: A heatwave and high wind can coincide. If a blind should never be forced shut while it is windy regardless of temperature, add a guard with policy: skip ahead of this rule's effect, or policy: force to fully open on wind — guards are evaluated after rules and can override what a heatwave rule decided.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A default that reads as "heatwave" when the sensor is missing — always pick the default that means "nothing unusual is happening".
  • A heatwave condition with no sun_hits_target pairing, closing the whole zone uniformly when only one facade actually needs it.
  • Expecting the rule to also protect against wind — temperature and wind are independent conditions; combine them explicitly if both matter.

docs.title: Migrate to Cover Logic
docs.text: Two starting points, two different paths. Both end the same way: Cover Logic holding every blind, nothing else sending cover.* commands to them.

docs.title: From hand-written automations
docs.text:
Cover Logic is built to run alongside whatever already controls your blinds, not to replace it on day one — shadow mode exists for exactly this. The migration path is:

  1. Set it up with dry_run on (the default) and build a configuration that covers everything your existing automations decide — see the concepts pages and the other how-to guides for the individual pieces (sun shading, heatwaves, door interlocks).
  2. Let both systems run side by side for at least a few days, spanning a dusk and a morning at minimum — the shadow mode checklist is the same list to work through here.
  3. Compare decisions, not just outcomes. Read sensor.cover_logic_mode's trace against what your automations actually did, from the logbook (/api/history/period with significant_changes_only=0 if you need attribute-only changes too). Agreement on why a blind moved matters as much as agreement on where it ended up — a rule that coincidentally reaches the same position for the wrong reason will diverge the next time something is different.
  4. Remove cover calls from the old automations one owner at a time, not all at once. Pick the automation that owns the fewest blinds or the simplest logic first, remove only its cover.* service calls (leaving anything else it does — notifications, other domains — untouched), and watch that specific set of blinds for a day before moving to the next owner. A blind briefly owned by nobody just sits still, which is safe; a blind owned by two systems at once is where surprises come from, so shrinking the overlap one automation at a time is what keeps the migration diagnosable if something looks wrong.
  5. Turn dry_run off once every blind has exactly one owner left: Cover Logic.

Keep the old automations disabled rather than deleted until you are confident — turning one back on is a safety net; reconstructing it from memory is not.

docs.title: From adaptive-cover
docs.text:
adaptive-cover runs one instance per window, each deciding a single climate-aware position from sun geometry. Cover Logic's model is different — several zones and modes live in one configuration — so migrating is a translation of concepts, not a field-for-field import. This table maps the adaptive-cover idea to its Cover Logic equivalent:

adaptive-cover concept Cover Logic equivalent Window azimuth facade_azimuth on the blind Field of view (FOV) tolerance on the blind, used by sun_hits_target Climate mode (shades when hot) A mode or rule with a numeric_state temperature condition — see heatwave Manual override manual_detection.hold Start/end time window A time condition (after/before), inline or as a named condition referenced with !ref

A few differences are worth knowing going in, not discovering midway:

  • One cover entity can only belong to one Cover Logic zone, but a zone can hold several blinds that should move together — where adaptive-cover had one instance per window, Cover Logic usually collapses several of those instances into one zone with one shared rule list, unless the windows genuinely need independent decisions.
  • Cover Logic has no built-in slat-angle-from-sun-elevation output the same way adaptive-cover's does by default — the equivalent is the slat_angle computed value, which derives a slat angle from the sun's elevation, its angle to the facade and the slat geometry. It has not been checked to give the same numbers as adaptive-cover, it is opt-in per !ref in a rule, and its slat-direction convention is unverified against real hardware — read that page's warning before relying on it.
  • A manual override in Cover Logic is detected from the cover's own state change, not configured as a separate per-window toggle — see manual moves for exactly what counts as manual, including its one real limitation (voice commands are not always detectable this way).

As with migrating from automations, do this with dry_run on first and compare before disabling the old integration's config entries — the same shadow mode checklist applies regardless of what you are migrating from.

docs.title: Shade a window when the sun hits it
docs.text:
The most common rule in this project: close a blind partway, angled, whenever the sun is actually on that side of the house — and leave it alone the rest of the time. This combines three concepts already covered on their own pages: a blind's facade azimuth, the sun_hits_target condition, and a rule that only partly acts (position: keep, only tilt set).

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.office_window
    facade_azimuth: 270 # west
    tolerance: 40
zones:
  office:
    members: [cover.office_window]
conditions:
  sun_up:
    condition: state
    entity_id: sun.sun
    state: above_horizon
  sun_on_this_facade:
    condition: sun_hits_target
modes:
  - id: home
rules:
  home.office:
    - if: {condition: and, conditions: [!ref sun_up, !ref sun_on_this_facade]}
      then: {position: keep, tilt: 15}
      name: afternoon sun, west-facing
    - then: {position: keep, tilt: keep}

docs.title: Why position: keep
docs.text: Height is a decision you usually want a person — or a different rule, like heatwave shading — to make. Shading from the sun is about angle, not height: leaving position at keep means this rule only ever touches the slats, and whatever else moved the blind up or down today is left alone. If you also want the blind to close by height when the sun hits it, set position to a number instead — nothing about sun_hits_target requires tilt-only.

docs.title: One rule works for every facade
docs.text: sun_hits_target reads facade_azimuth and tolerance off the blind currently being decided, not off the condition itself. The one rule above, written once under home.office, would work unchanged if copied to home.bedroom, home.kitchen, or any other zone — each blind supplies its own facing. Set up blinds now (see first setup) relies on the same property: its one shading rule covers every blind you give a compass direction, though it sets a fixed position 20 / tilt 45 rather than the tilt-only action above.

docs.title: Picking tolerance
docs.text: tolerance (default 45°) is how wide the "sun is on this facade" window is, centred on facade_azimuth. A narrower cone (shown here: 40°) means the blind reacts closer to when the sun is actually square-on to the window; a wider one reacts earlier in the morning and later in the evening, at the cost of catching more glancing, low-intensity sun. There is no universally right number — start at the default and narrow it if the blind reacts before direct sun is actually a problem.

docs.title: Adding a fallback for cloudy conditions
docs.text: sun_hits_target only looks at the sun's position, never at actual light levels — on an overcast day it will still fire exactly as it would in full sun, because geometrically the sun is still on that side of the sky. If you want the rule to stand down on a dim day, add a lux condition with and, the same way dusk by lux debounces a threshold — but be aware of the saturating-sensor trap that page explains before relying on one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting tolerance very wide and then being surprised the blind shades for most of the day — a wide cone is a wide cone on both sides of the bearing.
  • Forgetting the catch-all rule (then: {position: keep, tilt: keep}) at the end of the list — without it, the zone falls through to #none (equivalent in effect, but invisible in the trace as "nothing matched" rather than "this rule decided to do nothing").
  • Expecting this rule alone to protect against heat — it reacts to sun position only; pair it with heatwave if indoor temperature is the actual concern.

docs.title: Conditions reference
docs.text:
A condition answers true or false about the house at the moment of a recompute. Conditions appear in three places: a mode's when, a rule's if, and a guard's when. The dialect is a subset of Home Assistant's own condition syntax, plus three types of its own and two keys Home Assistant conditions do not have (for: and latch:).

A condition type not listed here, or one missing a required key, is an error when the configuration is validated (bad_condition_shape).

docs.title: Named conditions and !ref
docs.text:
The top-level conditions: mapping gives a condition a name, so it can be written once and reused anywhere a condition is accepted:

config
blinds:
  - entity: cover.office
zones:
  office:
    members: [cover.office]
conditions:
  door_open:
    condition: state
    entity_id: binary_sensor.office_door
    state: "on"
  dark:
    condition: numeric_state
    entity_id: sensor.outdoor_lux
    below: 2800
    default: 99999
  dark_and_closed:
    condition: and
    conditions: [!ref dark, {condition: not, conditions: [!ref door_open]}]
modes:
  - id: evening
    when: !ref dark_and_closed
  - id: day
rules:
  evening.office:
    - then: {position: 0, tilt: 0}
  day.office:
    - then: {position: 100, tilt: 100}
  • !ref <name> stands for the named condition's body. A named condition may reference another regardless of the order they are written in.
  • A !ref naming nothing is an error (unknown_condition_ref); a chain of references that leads back to itself is an error too (circular_condition_ref).
  • In the UI, named conditions are Add condition subentries.

A list written where one condition is expected means all of them must be true (an implicit and).

docs.title: Logic: and, or, not
docs.text:
type required true when and conditions every listed condition is true or conditions at least one listed condition is true not conditions none of the listed conditions is true

not over several conditions is not (A or B), as in Home Assistant — not not (A and B).

docs.title: state
docs.text:
key required meaning entity_id yes the entity to read state yes the value to match, or a list of values (any one matches) attribute no compare this attribute instead of the state for no seconds the entity must have been in its current state

for: is an extension: Home Assistant's own conditions have no for:. It is measured from the entity's last state change. If no change time is known, for: is ignored rather than failing the condition.

docs.title: numeric_state
docs.text:
key required meaning entity_id yes the entity to read above / below at least one strict bounds: value > above, value < below default yes the number used when the entity is missing, unknown, unavailable or not numeric attribute no read this attribute instead of the state for no seconds the threshold must stay crossed before it counts latch no only daily: once crossed, stay true until local midnight

default is required because there is no safe guess for it: pick the value that means "nothing unusual is happening" (see dusk by lux and heatwave). A node with default: also tells the readiness gate that a missing reading is acceptable.

for: qualifies the entry into the crossed state, and latch: daily refuses the exit; dusk by lux shows why a noisy sensor usually needs both. The memory behind for: and latch: lives only in the running integration: after a restart or reload, a for: dwell starts again from the first reading, and a latch that was holding is forgotten.

docs.title: time
docs.text:
key required meaning after at least one HH:MM or HH:MM:SS, local time, inclusive before at least one HH:MM or HH:MM:SS, local time, exclusive

When after is later than before (for example after: "22:00", before: "06:00"), the window wraps around midnight.

docs.title: sun
docs.text:
key required meaning after / before at least one sunrise or sunset after_offset / before_offset no offset in seconds (negative is earlier), not Home Assistant's "-00:20:00" string

before: sunrise together with after: sunset is the dark window around midnight. Where the sun does not rise or set that day, a condition naming the missing event is false.

docs.title: template
docs.text:
key required meaning value_template yes a Jinja template; true when it renders true, on, yes or 1

The template sees states(), is_state(), state_attr(), now() and today_at(), nothing else. Entity ids written literally in the template are watched, so a change to them triggers a recompute; an entity id the template computes is not.

docs.title: sun_hits_target
docs.text:
True when the sun is above the horizon and its azimuth lies within the decided blind's facade_azimuth ± tolerance (the lower edge included, the upper excluded). It reads the facing off the blind being decided, so one rule serves every facade — see shade by sun. A blind with no facade_azimuth never matches.

key default meaning sun_entity sun.sun must be above_horizon azimuth_entity sensor.sun_solar_azimuth where the sun's azimuth is read azimuth_attribute none read the azimuth from this attribute instead (for example azimuth on sun.sun) tolerance the blind's own tolerance override the half-width of the sector, in degrees

sensor.sun_solar_azimuth is disabled by default in Home Assistant; enable it, or use azimuth_entity: sun.sun with azimuth_attribute: azimuth as the starter setup does. A missing or out-of-range azimuth is false.

docs.title: manual_move
docs.text:
True when this recompute was prompted by a person moving the blind being decided (see manual moves for what is detected).

key default meaning direction any opening, closing or any

docs.title: event_targets_zone
docs.text: True when the event that prompted this recompute names a person listed in the decided zone's occupants. No keys. The running integration currently prompts recomputes only with state_change and manual_move events, which name no person, so in a live house this condition is not true yet.

docs.title: for: on other types
docs.text: Only state and numeric_state take for:. On any other type it is ignored and reported as the for_ignored warning.

YAML takes any number; 0 never matches, 180 or more always does. travel_time seconds 60 > 0 Time for a full run, used to wait for arrival before tilting.

docs.text: Field Type Default Range Meaning members list of entity ids none The blinds decided together as this zone. occupants list of person names none Person names read by the event_targets_zone condition (see conditions).
